info.description: Bounded simulator subset of the official Amazon Relational Database Service API (2014-10-31). Every other official operation returns HTTP 501 UnknownOperationException. By default, DB instances and DB clusters are stored configuration records that stay in the creating state: no database engine, storage, endpoint, address, port, listener, network interface, backup or monitoring exists, no endpoint, address or port is ever returned, and no SQL, Gremlin, SPARQL, openCypher or MongoDB data plane exists. DB subnet groups, DB parameter groups, DB cluster parameter groups and option groups are stored configuration too. Operations that act on a running database (RebootDBInstance, FailoverDBCluster, StartDBInstance, StopDBInstance, snapshots, restores, point-in-time restores, read replicas, promotion, switchover, backtrack, cluster activity streams, proxies, global clusters, blue/green deployments, event subscriptions) and every other official operation return UnknownOperationException with HTTP 501. The RDS API accepts no caller-supplied database credentials: MasterUserPassword, TdeCredentialPassword, TdeCredentialArn, ManageMasterUserPassword, RotateMasterUserPassword, MasterUserSecretKmsKeyId, DomainAuthSecretArn and PreSignedUrl are refused with InvalidParameterValue instead of being accepted and discarded, so a record is created with MasterUsername and no password (AWS would require a password or a managed secret). Port and DBPortNumber are refused because the RDS API exposes no configurable listener; Active Directory (Domain*), EC2-Classic DBSecurityGroups, renaming (NewDBInstanceIdentifier, NewDBClusterIdentifier), replication sources, global clusters, CloudwatchLogsExportConfiguration (use EnableCloudwatchLogsExports at creation) and deletion protection set to true (it is not enforced) are refused, and so is every member the official DB instance or DB cluster description does not hold. A record keeps exactly the settings it was given: the engine, version, instance class, storage, backup and maintenance windows, Availability Zone, encryption, monitoring and similar settings are stored without checking them against AWS offerings (no engine version, instance class or Region availability is validated) and no default is filled in. DBInstanceStatus and Status are creating from creation until deletion; ModifyDBInstance and ModifyDBCluster save metadata changes immediately. ApplyImmediately is accepted for SDK compatibility: it does not apply requested database settings or create pending values. Delete returns the record with status deleting. DB instance and DB cluster identifiers are 1 to 63 letters, digits or hyphens that start with a letter and neither end with a hyphen nor contain two consecutive hyphens, and are stored in lowercase; Engine must be a documented value (DB instances: aurora-mysql, aurora-postgresql, db2-ae, db2-se, docdb, mariadb, mysql, neptune, the oracle and sqlserver editions, postgres; DB clusters: aurora-mysql, aurora-postgresql, docdb, mysql, neptune, postgres); BackupRetentionPeriod is 0 to 35, PromotionTier 0 to 15 and MonitoringInterval one of 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 30 or 60. At most 40 DB instances and 40 DB clusters exist per Region (local limits). No snapshot can be taken, so deleting a DB instance or DB cluster refuses FinalDBSnapshotIdentifier and a SkipFinalSnapshot of false with InvalidParameterValue, and a DB cluster delete must also state SkipFinalSnapshot true. A DB instance delete may leave it out (the DocumentDB model has no such member, and AWS would otherwise demand a final snapshot name), which skips the snapshot. Neither the instances of a DB cluster nor the other direction is tracked: the records are independent, a DB instance may name a DBClusterIdentifier that does not exist, and a cluster is deletable while instances name it. In the default metadata-only mode, references to configuration groups are stored by name and not checked, because the engine cannot resolve a name held inside a nested member: the DB parameter group, option group, DB subnet group and VPC security group of a DB instance and the DB cluster parameter group, DB subnet group, option group and VPC security groups of a DB cluster need not exist, a group in use can be deleted, and a DB instance reports the configuration names with no VPC, subnets or Availability Zones. Group attachment here does not mean runtime settings were applied: DB instances with native RDS engines omit ParameterApplyStatus and option group Status, including for older stored records. Security group status remains active. The shared Aurora, Neptune and DocumentDB descriptions are unchanged. DB parameter group, option group and DB subnet group names given to an instance or cluster may also contain periods, so default.mysql8.0 is accepted. Parameter and option values are not modeled: ModifyDBParameterGroup, ResetDBParameterGroup, DescribeDBParameters, the cluster equivalents, CopyDBParameterGroup, ModifyOptionGroup and DescribeOptionGroupOptions are not implemented. Default parameter, option and subnet groups are not pre-created, and parameter group families, major engine versions and subnet IDs are stored without checking that they exist. In the default metadata-only mode, a subnet group needs 2 to 20 distinct subnet-xxxxxxxx or subnet-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx IDs and is not checked for Availability Zone coverage; it reports no VPC, Availability Zone, Outpost, status or network type. DB subnet group and DB (cluster) parameter group names are stored in lowercase as documented, "default" subnet groups are refused, and option groups accept only the documented EngineName values. Describe operations and ListTagsForResource refuse a non-empty Filters list (an empty one means no filter), Describe operations accept MaxRecords from 20 to 100 and fail with the operation's not-found fault for an unknown name, and DescribeOptionGroups refuses OptionGroupName together with EngineName or MajorEngineVersion. Tag keys are 1 to 128 and values at most 256 characters of letters, digits, spaces and _.:/=+-@, and neither may start with aws: or rds:. Tag operations on an unknown ARN fail with DBInstanceNotFound, the first not-found fault the official tag operations model. The optional --rds-private-postgres-topology setting validates qualifying standalone private PostgreSQL references against native EC2 topology. A separate --rds-owned-postgres-config option can admit one pinned PostgreSQL 15.20 workload on non-root Linux/amd64 with private persistent state and work directories. Only a qualifying authorized new DB instance generation can start that private process; authorized mutations retire it. Its fixed internal SCRAM-authenticated SQL probe does not add an RDS SQL API, published endpoint or port, caller credentials, guest connectivity, console controls, or a readiness claim: the RDS response remains creating. Default startup and topology validation alone start no database. Host-only SQL (#531: https://github.com/susumutomita/TenkaCloudSimulator/pull/531) and programmatic owned-generation checks (#543: https://github.com/susumutomita/TenkaCloudSimulator/pull/543) do not establish positive production CLI startup, guest SQL or end-to-end cleanup; the CLI opt-in retains those limits (#563: https://github.com/susumutomita/TenkaCloudSimulator/pull/563). Snapshots and restores remain unsupported. See docs/design/rds-owned-workload.md and docs/design/rds-owned-generation.md for prerequisites and limits. Amazon Aurora, Amazon Neptune and Amazon DocumentDB are managed through this same RDS API (Version 2014-10-31, signing name rds, rds: IAM actions, rds ARNs), and the boto3 neptune and docdb clients and the rds client with Aurora engines were run against these operations. Only configuration and records are served, not the products: no Aurora, Neptune or DocumentDB database, endpoint, snapshot or global cluster exists, no DB cluster or DB instance of those engines runs, and no SQL, Gremlin, SPARQL, openCypher or MongoDB data plane exists. The neptune client can use 21 of the 24 operations and the docdb client 18: neither model has option groups, and DocumentDB has no DB parameter groups. Parameter group families such as aurora-mysql8.0, neptune1.3 and docdb5.0 are stored without being checked. Responses omit SubnetOutpost, which the neptune and docdb models lack, and SupportedNetworkTypes, which the neptune model lacks. The RDS rules apply to every client: a non-empty Filters list is refused although those models define it, subnet group names must start with a letter although the neptune and docdb models do not say so, and tag keys and values may contain : and @, which the neptune and docdb models do not list.

tags.description: Bounded simulator subset of the official Amazon Relational Database Service API (2014-10-31). Every other official operation returns HTTP 501 UnknownOperationException. By default, DB instances and DB clusters are stored configuration records that stay in the creating state: no database engine, storage, endpoint, address, port, listener, network interface, backup or monitoring exists, no endpoint, address or port is ever returned, and no SQL, Gremlin, SPARQL, openCypher or MongoDB data plane exists. DB subnet groups, DB parameter groups, DB cluster parameter groups and option groups are stored configuration too. Operations that act on a running database (RebootDBInstance, FailoverDBCluster, StartDBInstance, StopDBInstance, snapshots, restores, point-in-time restores, read replicas, promotion, switchover, backtrack, cluster activity streams, proxies, global clusters, blue/green deployments, event subscriptions) and every other official operation return UnknownOperationException with HTTP 501. The RDS API accepts no caller-supplied database credentials: MasterUserPassword, TdeCredentialPassword, TdeCredentialArn, ManageMasterUserPassword, RotateMasterUserPassword, MasterUserSecretKmsKeyId, DomainAuthSecretArn and PreSignedUrl are refused with InvalidParameterValue instead of being accepted and discarded, so a record is created with MasterUsername and no password (AWS would require a password or a managed secret). Port and DBPortNumber are refused because the RDS API exposes no configurable listener; Active Directory (Domain*), EC2-Classic DBSecurityGroups, renaming (NewDBInstanceIdentifier, NewDBClusterIdentifier), replication sources, global clusters, CloudwatchLogsExportConfiguration (use EnableCloudwatchLogsExports at creation) and deletion protection set to true (it is not enforced) are refused, and so is every member the official DB instance or DB cluster description does not hold. A record keeps exactly the settings it was given: the engine, version, instance class, storage, backup and maintenance windows, Availability Zone, encryption, monitoring and similar settings are stored without checking them against AWS offerings (no engine version, instance class or Region availability is validated) and no default is filled in. DBInstanceStatus and Status are creating from creation until deletion; ModifyDBInstance and ModifyDBCluster save metadata changes immediately. ApplyImmediately is accepted for SDK compatibility: it does not apply requested database settings or create pending values. Delete returns the record with status deleting. DB instance and DB cluster identifiers are 1 to 63 letters, digits or hyphens that start with a letter and neither end with a hyphen nor contain two consecutive hyphens, and are stored in lowercase; Engine must be a documented value (DB instances: aurora-mysql, aurora-postgresql, db2-ae, db2-se, docdb, mariadb, mysql, neptune, the oracle and sqlserver editions, postgres; DB clusters: aurora-mysql, aurora-postgresql, docdb, mysql, neptune, postgres); BackupRetentionPeriod is 0 to 35, PromotionTier 0 to 15 and MonitoringInterval one of 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 30 or 60. At most 40 DB instances and 40 DB clusters exist per Region (local limits). No snapshot can be taken, so deleting a DB instance or DB cluster refuses FinalDBSnapshotIdentifier and a SkipFinalSnapshot of false with InvalidParameterValue, and a DB cluster delete must also state SkipFinalSnapshot true. A DB instance delete may leave it out (the DocumentDB model has no such member, and AWS would otherwise demand a final snapshot name), which skips the snapshot. Neither the instances of a DB cluster nor the other direction is tracked: the records are independent, a DB instance may name a DBClusterIdentifier that does not exist, and a cluster is deletable while instances name it. In the default metadata-only mode, references to configuration groups are stored by name and not checked, because the engine cannot resolve a name held inside a nested member: the DB parameter group, option group, DB subnet group and VPC security group of a DB instance and the DB cluster parameter group, DB subnet group, option group and VPC security groups of a DB cluster need not exist, a group in use can be deleted, and a DB instance reports the configuration names with no VPC, subnets or Availability Zones. Group attachment here does not mean runtime settings were applied: DB instances with native RDS engines omit ParameterApplyStatus and option group Status, including for older stored records. Security group status remains active. The shared Aurora, Neptune and DocumentDB descriptions are unchanged. DB parameter group, option group and DB subnet group names given to an instance or cluster may also contain periods, so default.mysql8.0 is accepted. Parameter and option values are not modeled: ModifyDBParameterGroup, ResetDBParameterGroup, DescribeDBParameters, the cluster equivalents, CopyDBParameterGroup, ModifyOptionGroup and DescribeOptionGroupOptions are not implemented. Default parameter, option and subnet groups are not pre-created, and parameter group families, major engine versions and subnet IDs are stored without checking that they exist. In the default metadata-only mode, a subnet group needs 2 to 20 distinct subnet-xxxxxxxx or subnet-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx IDs and is not checked for Availability Zone coverage; it reports no VPC, Availability Zone, Outpost, status or network type. DB subnet group and DB (cluster) parameter group names are stored in lowercase as documented, "default" subnet groups are refused, and option groups accept only the documented EngineName values. Describe operations and ListTagsForResource refuse a non-empty Filters list (an empty one means no filter), Describe operations accept MaxRecords from 20 to 100 and fail with the operation's not-found fault for an unknown name, and DescribeOptionGroups refuses OptionGroupName together with EngineName or MajorEngineVersion. Tag keys are 1 to 128 and values at most 256 characters of letters, digits, spaces and _.:/=+-@, and neither may start with aws: or rds:. Tag operations on an unknown ARN fail with DBInstanceNotFound, the first not-found fault the official tag operations model. The optional --rds-private-postgres-topology setting validates qualifying standalone private PostgreSQL references against native EC2 topology. A separate --rds-owned-postgres-config option can admit one pinned PostgreSQL 15.20 workload on non-root Linux/amd64 with private persistent state and work directories. Only a qualifying authorized new DB instance generation can start that private process; authorized mutations retire it. Its fixed internal SCRAM-authenticated SQL probe does not add an RDS SQL API, published endpoint or port, caller credentials, guest connectivity, console controls, or a readiness claim: the RDS response remains creating. Default startup and topology validation alone start no database. Host-only SQL (#531: https://github.com/susumutomita/TenkaCloudSimulator/pull/531) and programmatic owned-generation checks (#543: https://github.com/susumutomita/TenkaCloudSimulator/pull/543) do not establish positive production CLI startup, guest SQL or end-to-end cleanup; the CLI opt-in retains those limits (#563: https://github.com/susumutomita/TenkaCloudSimulator/pull/563). Snapshots and restores remain unsupported. See docs/design/rds-owned-workload.md and docs/design/rds-owned-generation.md for prerequisites and limits. Amazon Aurora, Amazon Neptune and Amazon DocumentDB are managed through this same RDS API (Version 2014-10-31, signing name rds, rds: IAM actions, rds ARNs), and the boto3 neptune and docdb clients and the rds client with Aurora engines were run against these operations. Only configuration and records are served, not the products: no Aurora, Neptune or DocumentDB database, endpoint, snapshot or global cluster exists, no DB cluster or DB instance of those engines runs, and no SQL, Gremlin, SPARQL, openCypher or MongoDB data plane exists. The neptune client can use 21 of the 24 operations and the docdb client 18: neither model has option groups, and DocumentDB has no DB parameter groups. Parameter group families such as aurora-mysql8.0, neptune1.3 and docdb5.0 are stored without being checked. Responses omit SubnetOutpost, which the neptune and docdb models lack, and SupportedNetworkTypes, which the neptune model lacks. The RDS rules apply to every client: a non-empty Filters list is refused although those models define it, subnet group names must start with a letter although the neptune and docdb models do not say so, and tag keys and values may contain : and @, which the neptune and docdb models do not list.
